title: SYSK Selects: How Commercial Jingles Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on commercial jingles. Josh introduces it as a Selects pick, then the hosts cover what a jingle is (slogans, phone numbers, call letters, audio branding), the Wheaties Quartet as an early jingle, the 1905 song "In My Merry Oldsmobile" as a licensed pop song rather than a true jingle, 1930s radio sponsorship and the rise of jingles, psychology of advertising, what makes a jingle memorable (repetition, rhyme, simplicity), the Oscar Mayer bologna song, earworms and the phonological loop from Baddeley and Hitch, Professor Ira Hirschfeld-style earworm research (Playlist from Hell), tips for getting rid of earworms, licensing pop songs in ads (VW, Nike, Timberland, Jaguar and Sting, Chevy and Band of Horses, Black Keys vs. Pizza Hut), product placement, and a listener mail request for Free IT Athens.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode on commercial jingles and earworms. The hosts chat about Mystery Science Theater 3000, Barry Manilow's jingle work, and Lynn Duddy.

segments.title: Defining the commercial jingle and audio branding
segments.summary: A jingle is a memorable melody about a product, and can include slogans, phone numbers, call letters, or benefit claims. Audio branding, such as NBC chimes and computer startup sounds, is a related modern concept. Early examples like Crest Patrol cartoons are mentioned.

segments.title: Early jingles: Wheaties Quartet and In My Merry Oldsmobile
segments.summary: The Wheaties Quartet is credited with cereal's first jingle, which reportedly saved Wheaties. The 1905 song 'In My Merry Oldsmobile' is described as an early licensed pop song rather than a true jingle.

segments.title: 1930s radio sponsorship and the rise of jingles
segments.summary: Consumer protection rules limited direct advertising in the 1930s, so advertisers sponsored whole radio programs, which led to shows like The Shadow and later TV programming. Ads shifted from dry, bullet-pointed claims to catchy music, and psychologists began advising advertisers.

segments.title: What makes a jingle memorable and the Oscar Mayer song
segments.summary: Simplicity, repetition, and rhyme help jingles stick. The Oscar Mayer bologna song is cited as an example many people can sing from childhood.

segments.title: Earworms and the phonological loop
segments.summary: Earworms are songs or snippets stuck in the head. Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model includes the phonological loop, which the hosts link to why earworms persist. Earworms may be more common among women, musicians, and people with OCD.

segments.title: Playlist from Hell and removing earworms
segments.summary: Professor Cohen's survey-based Playlist from Hell includes songs like Chili's jingle, Who Let the Dogs Out, Queen's We Will Rock You, Kit Kat, Mission Impossible theme, YMCA, The Lion Sleeps Tonight, and It's a Small World. Tips for removing earworms are discussed, such as hearing or singing the song through.

segments.title: Licensing pop songs in ads and sync controversies
segments.summary: Brands increasingly use popular songs rather than jingles, as with VW's Nick Drake use, Nike's Revolution, Timberland, Jaguar's use of Sting's Desert Rose, and Chevy's use of Band of Horses. The hosts criticize sound-alike remakes and mention the Black Keys suing Pizza Hut and Ray Parker Jr.'s 'Ghostbusters' case.

segments.title: Product placement and Soap Opera Cereal
segments.summary: The hosts discuss product placement in TV shows as a response to DVR ad-skipping, and mention the Soap Opera Cereal YouTube video.

segments.title: Listener mail: Free IT Athens
segments.summary: A listener from Athens, Georgia asks listeners to support Free IT Athens, a volunteer nonprofit that refurbishes donated computers for low-income people, and seeks working laptops made within the last five years. The hosts close by asking for listener jingles.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, invite jingle submissions, and give social media and website information.
